analysis.one_liner: Caps out-of-pocket insulin costs at $35 a month for insured people and subsidizes insulin for the uninsured.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2026 with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate health committee and has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require private health plans to cover at least one insulin product of each type and dosage form without applying a deductible, and cap what a patient pays for a month's supply at $35 or 25% of the plan's negotiated price, whichever is less. It would also require high-deductible and catastrophic plans to cover insulin before the deductible kicks in. For people with no insurance, the government would pay pharmacies and doctors the difference between what the insulin costs the patient and $35.
analysis.who_benefits: People with diabetes who use insulin. Insured patients would stop paying full price for insulin before meeting their deductible, and high-deductible plan enrollees would get insulin covered up front. Uninsured people could get insulin at no more than $35 a month from participating pharmacies and providers, with the federal government covering the rest.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured and uninsured people who use insulin

how_it_helps.text: Private plans, including employer plans and individual market plans, could not apply a deductible to selected insulin products and could not charge more than $35 per 30-day supply, or 25% of the negotiated net price if that is lower, starting in 2027 [S2][S3].
High-deductible health plans and catastrophic plans would have to cover selected insulin products before the patient reaches the deductible [S3].

HHS would set up a program paying pharmacies and health care providers the difference between an uninsured patient's out-of-pocket insulin cost and $35, with the provider barred from billing the patient for the rest [S2][S3].
Patient cost-sharing for insulin would count toward deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums, and the insulin carve-out would not reduce a plan's measured actuarial value [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health plans and insurers absorb the difference between current insulin cost-sharing and the $35 cap, and the federal government pays the full gap for uninsured people. The bill contains no offset for the federal cost; its only fiscal provision is a statement that Congress should pass one later [S3]. Some of the plan-side cost is likely to show up in premiums, and because the uninsured program reimburses whatever the insulin's out-of-pocket price is, drug makers' high list prices would be paid with taxpayer dollars rather than lowered.

drawbacks.text: The bill includes no offset for the federal cost of the uninsured program; Congress only states that a later bill should provide one, so the spending would add to the deficit unless offset separately [S3].

The uninsured program pays pharmacies and providers whatever the insulin costs above $35, so it subsidizes demand without lowering manufacturers' prices, making taxpayers rather than drug makers absorb the high list price [S3].
Each plan chooses which insulin products count as 'selected,' so plans could steer patients to particular products, and the caps do not apply to insulin from out-of-network providers [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that insurers' added costs may be passed back to everyone through premiums, and that a single-sponsor bill with no cosponsors is unlikely to become law in this form.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly eight million Americans who use insulin, the caps would be a real and immediate benefit, ending the common situation where insulin costs hundreds of dollars before a deductible is met. The design has real weaknesses: the uninsured program subsidizes high drug prices instead of negotiating them down, the federal cost is deliberately left unoffset, and plans keep control over which insulins get the cap. On balance the patient-facing benefits are clear and the costs are diffuse, but the bill's one-sponsor start makes its passage unlikely without substantial changes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate in May 2026, read twice, and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote; Congress is still in session, so it could still move.

narrative.text: Sen. John Kennedy introduced S. 4512 on May 13, 2026 [S1][S5].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; that is the last action on record [S5].
No senators from either party have cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet, because nothing has happened. Insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, and insulin manufacturers continue operating under today's pricing and cost-sharing rules, and insulin users continue paying whatever their plans and pharmacies charge.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; current pricing rules stand

for.name: Sen. John Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Louisiana; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and saw it referred to the Senate HELP Committee.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator introduced the bill but no Democrat or additional Republican has signed on, so no partisan pattern has formed.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: Plans would have to cover insulin without a deductible and cap patient cost-sharing at $35 a month, absorbing the difference; some of that cost would likely shift into premiums. Their interest in the bill's fate runs against the benefit to insulin users.

The private-insurance cap does not set drug prices and plans must cover at least one product per type, so manufacturers keep most of their market. The uninsured program actually pays out whatever the out-of-pocket price is above $35 with federal money, so high list prices get reimbursed rather than reduced.
Qualifying pharmacies and providers would receive a new federal reimbursement stream for furnishing insulin to uninsured patients, with the government covering everything above $35.

The 25% cap is calculated on the negotiated price net of all price concessions, including those received by PBMs, so larger PBM discounts would push the patient cap lower; the bill otherwise leaves the PBM rebate system intact.
The uninsured-insulin program would be paid out of federal funds with no offset in the bill itself, only a sense of Congress that offsets should come later.

analysis.trajectory: A single-sponsor bill referred to committee late in a Congress, with zero cosponsors from either party, very rarely reaches the floor. Unless Sen. Kennedy attracts cosponsors and the HELP Committee takes it up, the bill will most likely die in committee when this Congress ends in January 2027; similar insulin cost-sharing caps have advanced only when attached to larger packages.
